entries.title: Moment truncation controls variance without proving a spectral rate [draft; pending w347]
entries.statement: If eps>0 and M=E|X|^(2+eps)<infinity, then E[|X|^2 1_{|X|>R}]<=M*R^(-eps) for R>0. The power eps is sharp as a scalar envelope: a symmetric atom law with total mass c*2^(-(2+eps)*j)/j^2 at +/-2^j has finite (2+eps)-moment and tail variance of order 2^(-eps*m)/m^2 at R=2^m. This proves neither a lower bound nor an optimal exponent for a circular-law convergence rate.
entries.proof_text:
For eps>0, R>0 and M=E|X|^(2+eps)<infinity,

    E[|X|^2 * 1_{|X|>R}] <= M*R^(-eps),
    P(|X|>R) <= M*R^(-(2+eps)).

These follow pointwise from |X|^2<=R^(-eps)|X|^(2+eps) on the tail, and Markov's inequality. At R=n^r the first bound is M*n^(-r*eps). It bounds a truncation error; it is not a lower bound for the error of the original matrix's empirical eigenvalue law.

The power eps in the scalar tail envelope cannot be uniformly increased under the same moment assumption. Take a symmetric law with total probability q_j=c*2^(-(2+eps)*j)/j^2 at the two atoms +/-2^j, j>=1, and remaining mass at zero, choosing c>0 sufficiently small. It has mean zero, positive finite variance and finite (2+eps)-moment c*sum_j j^(-2). At R=2^m, its missing variance is

    c*sum_{j>m} 2^(-eps*j)/j^2.

The first summand gives a lower bound; a geometric series after replacing j by m gives an upper bound. For m>=1 this quantity lies between positive constants times 2^(-eps*m)/m^2. Thus it is not O(R^(-eps-eta)) for any eta>0 along dyadic cutoffs. Rescaling by its standard deviation preserves the tail exponent. This sharpness statement concerns a scalar truncation envelope and does not prove a moment-dependent circular-law lower bound.
assumptions: Tail sharpness concerns scalar laws only

entries.title: Rank-one perturbations can move a nonnormal spectral law by one [draft; pending w347]
entries.statement: For n>=2, let J_n be the nilpotent matrix with ones on the superdiagonal, and C_n=J_n+e_n e_1^T. Their difference has rank one, but the empirical eigenvalue laws differ by one on the bounded 1-Lipschitz test f(z)=min(|z|,1): J_n has only zero eigenvalues and C_n has all nth roots of unity. Thus a Hermitian-style rank/n bound cannot control nonnormal empirical eigenvalue laws in general. This deterministic example is not an iid circular-law lower bound.
entries.proof_text: J_n^n=0. For every z with z^n=1, C_n(1,z,...,z^(n-1))=z(1,z,...,z^(n-1)); these are n distinct eigenvalues. The perturbation is the single nonzero outer product e_n e_1^T. The radial test is zero at the origin and one at each root of unity.
assumptions: Bounded Lipschitz comparison of eigenvalue laws
